docs.title: License to Drill Act
s: Madam President, first, I would like to say that my colleague from Utah was out here a minute ago.
We often disagree on many things, but every now and then, we agree on something.

I just want to say how grateful I am that the Senate, today, passed by unanimous consent a bill that we have been working on for years and years and years, with the community around Crystal Reservoir, to make sure that that can be transferred from the Forest Service to the people of Ouray, who desperately, desperately need it.
I am grateful that we were able to get this done, and we will continue to work on this together to make sure we get it passed in the House of Representatives.
So it is a bright light in an otherwise not so bright day legislatively around here in the U.S. Senate.
Madam President, I wanted to come to the floor because today may be the end of the opportunity to talk on the Senate floor for this session of the Senate before we recess for the coming elections.
I wish that there was a lot of stuff that we had addressed together.
The American people are struggling with costs and this economy in a way that they have never struggled before, and that is not an exaggeration.
It is true in rural Colorado and in urban Colorado.
It is true in Republican parts of the State and in Democratic parts of the State.
It doesn't matter.

People--no matter how hard they work--feel like they can't get ahead and their kids can't live better lives than the lives that they are leading; that no matter how hard they work, it is becoming harder and harder and, in some ways, impossible--impossible--to live a middle class life anymore.

For the kids who are graduating from high school right now in America and for the kids who are graduating from college in America, it feels like the American dream is further and further and further out of reach because it is.
It is.
I see the pages who are sitting here on this floor today.
They are the first generation of Americans since forever--I don't want to depress you tonight, but I guess I can tell you the truth so you can help fix it.
They are the first generation of Americans who are likely to earn less than their parents earned if we don't change it.
We are living in a world where people who are 30--a lot older than the pages who are here today--on average, are going to earn less than their parents earned.

We are living in a time when 1 percent of the American people own 50 percent of the value of the stock market, and the bottom 50 percent of the American people own 1 percent of the value of the stock market.
If you have not been somebody in the United States who owns assets--who owns real estate, who owns stocks and bonds--it has been a tough 15 years or 20 years.
It has actually been tough going all the way back to Ronald Reagan, to be honest, when these trickle-down policies started.
Ronald Reagan was certainly a purveyor of these.
You know, he put in place a lot of the tax cuts and other things that were kind of the beginning of trickle-down economics.
I don't think even he could have foreseen what the Trump administration would have done to pursue the kind of trickle-down economics that they have pursued.

It has been like a raging forest fire that has gone across the United States of America at a time when our inequality is growing; at a time when Reagan could never have imagined, I don't think, the wealth inequality that we now have in this country, the lack of economic mobility we have in what I still refer to as the “land of opportunity” because, in the end, I am relentlessly hopeful about where this country is headed.
But the reality is--the reality is--unless you are at the very top of this economy for decades, you have not done well and your kids have done worse.
That is the opposite of the American dream.

I am sorry to say this to the pages that are here, but there was a time in American history--when I was your age, for example--when we took it as a given that each generation was going to benefit from the work of the previous generation, and the greatest gift we could give the next generation was more prosperity than our generation had.

My daughters are now in their midtwenties--actually, to be honest, the youngest is in her early twenties--but my daughters are now in their midtwenties, and they are really serious about the question, which I am not going to repeat on this floor because I would be thrown out for using “W-T.”
That is their view, though.
That is their view because they know a lot about history.
They know what the transition was from one generation to the next.
They know what the solemn responsibility of every American generation was.
And now they find themselves and their whole generation finds themselves completely ignored by this Congress, completely ignored by the President of the United States.
He could care less about their future.
I used to be a superintendent of schools in Denver before I came here.
I was in business before that.
I have had kind of a checkered career on the way to the U.S. Senate.

And I can tell you, I can assure you that President Trump does not see the families of the kids I used to work for in the Denver public schools, who are working two and three jobs just to feed their children, who are working two and three jobs just to keep a roof over their heads, just to pay the rent in this economy, this savage economy they are facing.
I am sorry to say this to the pages as well.
The Trump administration is breaking new records every week.
Gas prices are up 42 percent from the year before.
Diesel is the highest it has ever been in American history at $6.50 a gallon.
It has never been higher.

There are farmers and ranchers all over Colorado who have had to put thousands and thousands and thousands of incremental dollars, of extra dollars they don't have, dollars they need to invest in their own kids' future, dollars they need to invest in their own businesses--they are having to burn it in their tractors because Donald Trump decided to go to war in Iran--against the advice of all of his advisers, by the way, who told him that if you drop bombs on the mullahs, they are not going to abdicate; who told him that if you drop bombs on the mullahs, there won't be a regime change, and, in fact, the people that come will be more radical than the ones you are attacking; who told him that they would close the Strait of Hormuz; who told him that you better watch out, Mr. President, because you might be facing--and since you don't probably drive a tractor, you may not care as much, but the farmers and ranchers all over America are going to be facing diesel prices that are $6.50; that it will be the difference between their ability to afford healthcare or invest in their business or pay for their kid to go to higher education, to learn a trade.
That is all going away because of these insane prices--gas prices up 42 percent and diesel at $6.50.
Now, something that is hard to understand for some people around here is the effect of these interest rates, which are hitting some of the highest levels we have seen in decades.
The 10-year yield is the highest level since 2007--20 years ago, two decades ago.
You have to go back 20 years to get to an interest rate like this.
The 30-year reached its highest level since June 2002.
That is a catastrophe for anybody in this economy who is trying to borrow money.
This is a catastrophe for anybody in this economy who is trying to pay a mortgage on a house.

Mortgage rates are now over 7 percent in the United States of America because of Donald Trump's policies, because he invaded Iran, because--I have to say both parties are somewhat responsible for this.
My friend that I respect so much from Oklahoma is here.
By the way, my oldest daughter is living happily--happily--in Tulsa, OK, because she can pay I think 28 percent of her income in housing.
She is very, very happy to be there at a time when, in lots of other places, no one, you know, who is her contemporary, who went to college with her, can afford to pay to live anywhere.
So she is delighted to have a chance to be there, to be working in Tulsa.
But for people that are trying to buy a house in America, for her generation, rates are now at 7 percent, and none of them can afford to buy a house.
And what did that do?
Yes, the loans went to zero as well--they were low--but the price of housing went through the roof; the stock market went through the roof.
Anybody who had assets, anybody who was rich, anybody who had a fancy house anywhere in America benefited hugely.
We are in that moment again.
We are in that moment again, the moment we have been in for almost 50 years in America.
When the economy grows, the wealthiest people do incredibly well, and for everyone else, it is like a recession.
In fact, it is a recession.
It is a recession.
When there are recessions in America today, those are real recessions for working people and for poor people.
For wealthy people, that is a period of economic growth.
Our Nation has detached the wealthiest people.
It is like they are in a capsule floating above all of us.
They are in a capsule floating above all of us, and when the economy does well, they do great; when the economy does poorly, they do poorly.

I wish everybody well, everyone in this economy, but the reality for everybody else--in fact, I don't think it is an exaggeration to say that for 95 percent of Americans, for decades, the periods of economic growth have basically acted as recessions, and recessions have been devastating.

For the next generation of Americans, for my kids' generation, they can't even get a glimmer of economic prosperity, where their share of the American dream is going to come from, their opportunity to be able to participate meaningfully in this democracy and in this economy.
And they are all smart.
They are all--my daughter will get mad at me, but she is teaching a history class at a community college in Tulsa.
And they know the history of this Nation.
They know we have been a nation that stood for freedom and for opportunity for all these years.
But something is broken in the way this works, and it doesn't work for them.

If you wonder, by the way, why we are facing all this division and chaos in our politics, if you wonder why we seem to be living in a moment when no one in this Chamber can work together and where the American people are--at least the ones that are on their social media--are relentlessly at war with each other on that social media, there might be a lot of reasons, but I am telling you the real reason is because we have lost the sense of economic opportunity in the Nation because we don't really have it anymore for the people that are coming after us, and our gaps in wealth are just getting larger and larger and larger and larger.
The chance for people to get ahead is getting harder and harder and harder.
That always breeds politics of division; that always breeds the politics of chaos.
I wish Donald Trump were interested in any of this, except for the division and the chaos.

His politics has been a politics of sowing division, of sowing chaos, of preying on the divisions we have, and we have, unfortunately, fallen into that trap at a time when America actually needs us to be solving the problems they are facing, and I think a lot of folks feel like we have just given up on it.
Our kids are reading--our literacy levels in America are worse than they were 30 years ago, and they were low 30 years ago.
We spend twice as much as any other industrialized country on healthcare, and we get much worse results.
When Ronald Reagan--I mentioned him earlier--when he was President, we had the same life expectancy of everybody in the world.
Now we are 6 or 7 years behind the industrialized world here in the United States.
If you are African American in this country, whether you live in Oklahoma or Colorado, your life expectancy is even shorter than that.
The good news is that there is no shortage of challenges we could confront.
I will give you another one that I know my colleague cares about and I care about.
We now have $40 trillion of debt on the balance sheet of this country--$40 trillion.
That is one of the reasons why interest rates are going up the way they are.
From my daughters Caroline, Halina, and Anne's perspective, their generation's perspective, they look at that and say: What did we get for that?
You guys went out and borrowed $40 trillion.
Like you put the biggest mortgage that you could ever pull out of a bank on the United States of America.
Imagine if our country were a big house, and you went out there and took a $40 trillion mortgage on it, and then you built yourself a swimming pool, and you built yourself a bunch of statues.

I suppose, in the case of Donald Trump, you bought yourself a bunch of gilded stuff that you hung in the Oval Office or tried to knock Jack Kennedy's name off the Kennedy Center by putting your name up there, which doesn't deserve to be up there.
It shouldn't be up there.
You spent your time building statues and layering them in gold leaf.
The next generation of Americans might rightly say: You borrowed $40 trillion for this?
The reality is that all of that pales in comparison to the tax cuts these guys have given to the wealthiest people in this country without paying for it.

All of that pales--and I just want to be honest and admit that it pales in comparison to the $8 trillion we essentially lit on fire in the Middle East to pay for two forever wars there that, by the way, President Trump said he would never repeat.
He got elected--actually, Barack Obama got elected by first saying: I am not against all wars, but I am against dumb wars.
He found a way to jump a whole generation of politicians to become President on the strength of that argument.
Donald Trump made a very similar argument, which is: No more long wars.
No more forever wars.
Now he has created one.
This war of choice in Iran is going to be a war that ends when the mullahs decide.
That is a long war.
That is a long war.
I have a long memory.
I can remember.
I can remember.
This is long before you guys were born.
I remember when our folks--our diplomats were taken hostage in Tehran.
These are the people we are dealing with.
He is consuming, by the way, missile after missile after missile that is really important to our deterrence of China and in the Pacific theater.
And he hasn't paid for a single dollar of that--not a dollar, not a dollar.
That is the best way for us to end this war.
That has happened before.
We are not powerless.
The U.S. Senate is not powerless.
People on this floor, in both parties, they brought the Vietnam war to an end by saying: We are going to cut it off if you don't stop.
And we are in that position today.
I would be shocked if there is anybody over there who really supports what the President has done in Iran.
I certainly can't find anybody in Colorado who is a Republican, a Democrat or unaffiliated--almost anybody, almost anybody--a handful who believe this was a good idea, especially the next generation.

And certainly not our farmers and ranchers, who are facing higher input, as I said, and now higher borrowing costs because of this President's policies and weakening commodity prices, because we have a completely incoherent trade policy.
Xi Jinping was just over here.
Donald Trump did nothing to get him to buy our soybeans.
And, by the way, having said that he was going to do something about it, he has now allowed Brazil to come and steal our business, which they are doing.
Exports are incredibly important to our farmers, incredibly important to our ranchers, and Donald Trump has cut them off for his ridiculous trade wars.
And I have said for years on this floor: We have to take China on.
We have to take China on.
But we have to do it in a smart way, not in a stupid way, not in an incoherent way, not in a way that gives Brazil the opportunity to knock our farmers out of the picture.

And I will say that everything that I said earlier about the difficulties of the next generation of Americans, the difficulties of the generation of kids that I used to work for in the Denver Public Schools--all of it is magnified if you live in rural America, if you live in rural Colorado, because it is just harder when you have fewer people.
Healthcare is more expensive.
Childcare is more expensive.
Groceries are more expensive.
Gas is more expensive.
Everything is harder, and you have to travel long distances to get places.
And now, everyone in America is spending more.
Families are forced to pay more for everything.
They are paying more on gas.
Bags of groceries are a month's rent now or more.
People are having to make choices between buying their kids clothes for school and buying groceries.
There are hundreds of more dollars that people are having to spend on electricity and on housing itself and rent.
I haven't heard President Trump talk about any of this because the next generation is entirely invisible to him.
He has no concern about it.
He is not worried about it.
That is not of his concern.
Every day he parades what his real interests are across the front pages of what is left of the newspapers of America and the television and his social media feed.
And he is proud of it, by the way.
He is proud of it.
So I know, when I talk about this, if he hears about it, he will say: Oh, I got his goat.
Well, that is what I wanted to do.
And he is.
He is proud of his corruption.
He is proud.
He wears it on his sleeve.
The latest of this was that he has now spent millions of taxpayer dollars on political advertisements--millions of taxpayer dollars on political advertisements.
I would be surprised if there is anybody here who supports that.
We have 330 million Americans.

Of that, all but three think that it is a bad idea to use their money--to use taxpayer money--when we have $40 trillion of debt, when we have 7 percent interest rates, when diesel is $6.50 a gallon, and that the President is using our money to pay for ads for his reelection and the election of people in his party in this midterm.
He is hanging his photograph, his picture, on the outside of the Federal Agencies here in Washington, DC.

That is not the worst thing that he has done, but it does make me feel, every time I drive through it, like we are living in an occupied state, like we are living in North Korea or Beijing or some other place where the great leader is respected because he tells everybody in the country how they are supposed to think about everything.
I know he thinks he is the greatest President in American history.
I know he does.
He has even said that.
I think he thinks he is greater than George Washington.
None of those people put their pictures on the outside of these buildings.
None of these people tried to hang their name next to Jack Kennedy's name or put their photo on the Department of Justice or the Department of Labor.

But part of his renovation of this town has been a billion dollars in White House renovations, including his ballroom and his helipad--a billion dollars that he has spent on the ballroom and the helipad.
And he has cheerfully basically admitted that he has made $1.4 billion in crypto profits while being President of the United States, and his family has made untoward amounts.
And he has relationships, the President, all over the world that are helping him pursue those economic interests while he is in the White House.
I know we are living at a really unusual time in American history.
I know we are living in a time when there is enormous frustration, when there is enormous anger, when there is a lot of division and distrust.
I know we are.
But I think it is fair to say that most Americans don't want their Presidents to get rich when they come to office.

I think that most Americans know that no President has ever gotten rich the way Donald Trump has, when they can't even afford to pay the rent, when they can't even afford to buy shoes for their kids and give them school uniforms.
They know no President has put their own face on the outside of these buildings, like this is some cult of personality instead of what it is, which is the American democracy.

I think that most people in America are going to say that they don't really want to live in a country where Federal law enforcement wearing masks can show up in your neighborhood and bang on your door and drag you out of your house, which Donald Trump has also done.
I know that no American would agree--no American would agree--that any President should weaponize the Federal Government for his own political purposes.

This is not a country where, you know, if one party loses and the other one wins, that the one that wins uses its office to weaponize the power of the Federal Government against States that didn't vote for them or disagree with them.
And I am telling you, folks, that if we fall into that trap of treating that as the new normal, we are going to be here for a really long time because this is how democracies and republics die.

This is how they spin out of control, when we jeopardize our values and our beliefs for a set of behaviors that are just totally out of the mainstream of American history--in this case, the weaponization of politics.
Colorado has witnessed a form of this firsthand.
The administration canceled $109 million of transportation grants.
The President denied disaster declarations for the Elk and Lee Fires in Rio Blanco County, and for flooding in Western Colorado.
They tried to block 100,000 families from receiving SNAP benefits.
They have tried to dismantle the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Boulder.
And most shamefully--I mean, that is a long list.

But most shamefully, they stole the promise of clean drinking water from 50,000 Coloradans in the southeastern part of my State who have been waiting for decades for the Federal Government to finally finish a project that was promised by Jack Kennedy when he went out to Pueblo in 1960 and promised it to the farmers and ranchers there.
We have passed it unanimously in the Senate.
We have passed it unanimously in the House.
And yet President Trump has taken it away.

So not only is he focused on the things that won't make our economy better, not only is he not focused on the next generation of Americans, not only is he not saying to himself, “What do I do every day to try to deal with the costs that people are facing and the affordability crisis?”--it is a crisis that they are facing--he is making matters worse.
It is like he is going out of his way to make everybody's life harder and worse.
I would be shocked if there are people here who actually support what he is doing in Iran.
I know the American people don't.

And it is not just because it is crushing them economically because of what the mullahs are doing with energy prices and what they are doing with--not them but what the war is doing with interest rates.
It is not just because of that.
It is because they can see how ridiculous this is--the lack of strategy, the lack of focus.

They know that he snatched Maduro in the middle of the night and that somehow he decided that dropping the bombs on Iran was going to get the same result, even when all the intelligence said: That is not what is going to happen.
You are not going to replace the regime.
You are not going to be able to take away their nuclear weapons from the air.
They are going to constrict oil from the Middle East.
There isn't anyone in the Middle East that doesn't think they are not going to be paying tolls from now until eternity to the Iranians, to the mullahs, because of what Donald Trump has done.
It is ridiculous.
It is not just a war of choice.
It is a war that has created catastrophe for the American people.
We have lost the lives of soldiers in this country.

They have bombed our military bases and the bases of our neighbors--which, by the way, our intelligence Agencies said they would--and now they are in a better negotiating position than they were before the war was started.
And now they have people in charge that are actually more attached, if you can believe it, more attached to the prospect of getting nuclear weapons than the people that they replaced.
As I said earlier, he has put us in a worse position with China.
Xi Jinping shows up here, and the President goes and meets him at the airport and drives him back to the White House and genuflects over and over and over to him.
And I can guarantee you, Xi Jinping was happy to be feted this way by the President of the United States because he knows how much advantage he is taking of the President.
The Iran war has been a huge boon to China--and to Russia, by the way.
It has put them in a much better position than they were in before he started.
The Ukrainians, with no help basically from the President, finally had Putin on his heels.
And they are doing an unbelievable job.
We all owe them a huge debt of gratitude.
And then President Trump gives Putin the gift of invading Iran, the gift of driving these people into each other's corner.
I mentioned his incoherent trade war with the entire world.
We are basically tariffing the entire world, and that is haunting our farmers and ranchers.
It is crushing our small business owners all over Colorado--and consumers as well.
Consumer sentiment is at the second lowest point in 70 years.
Please stop, Mr. President.
Stop.
We cannot afford your policies anymore.
We are trying to raise our kids, build our small businesses, turn something over to the next generation that we are proud of.
People are stuck in the jobs that they are in because there is nowhere for them to move.
The hire rates in America are at record lows.
No one can buy a house because of interest rates.
And, by the way, seniors who would like to maybe downsize and move out of their house so that my kids' generation can move in, they can't do anything.
They can't go anywhere.
And in many ways those folks, our seniors on fixed incomes, they are in as rough a position as anybody because of his policies.
But let me tell the Presiding Officer this.

Here is what is happening in Donald Trump's economy right now: Forty-two percent of the recent college graduates in America--42 percent--are underemployed, and their peers are in even worse shape in this country.
That is a hard way to start your life.
If you are a young man in America today in your twenties, you are making 40 percent less in real dollars than you were in 1976--40 percent less in inflation-adjusted dollars than you were in 1976.
There is no way--no wonder people are getting stuck in their parents' basement.
By the way, nothing would fill me with greater joy than having my own daughters move back into my basement, but I get the idea that kids don't want to do that.
They want to start their lives.
They want to start their businesses.
They want to be able to afford higher education, which they can't.
And now, even if they get it, 42 percent of them are underemployed.
I will just finish.
I know that I have colleagues who want to talk.

But let me just say one other thing that has been in the news lately that the President has been happily making news about, which is this whole issue of AI, which is part of the economic anxiety that especially the next generation is feeling--and for good reason.
They are worried about what this is going to mean for their jobs and the economy.
That is not irrational.
That is why I put out language last week to create a new Federal Agency to actually negotiate with these guys.
No one in America has had a negotiation with Mark Zuckerberg over anything.
We haven't had a negotiation about our privacy, our data, our kids' mental health, our economic interests.
This Congress 15 years ago should have put this in place to deal with, if nothing else, the mental health issues that have been afflicting our kids because of these social media platforms.
But now, with AI, it is clear we have to have--Congress is never going to be able to figure it out.
States can't regulate it.
We have Anthropic, one of the leading American companies, says that its technology poses an “existential risk to humanity.”
That is what they wrote.
That is what they wrote.
I think about the lawyers that are drafting this stuff for the AI companies that are having to put in it that the technology is potentially an existential risk to humanity.
And I wonder, if the worst happens, who they think is going to be there to sue them if they don't put that language in.
But that is where we are.
That is what the industry is saying itself.
The President has responded with his “morally binding” agreement with the AI companies and themselves, calling fears over AI a “hoax”--a “hoax.”
We could fix that here.
We could create a new Agency in America to have that negotiation with Zuckerberg and the rest of these guys, just like Teddy Roosevelt did, Franklin Roosevelt did.
There is a reason we don't have planes dropping out of the sky.
There is a reason why we know our drugs are safe.
There is a reason why we have been able to proceed with our nuclear weapons and nuclear technology without destroying ourselves.

It is because we came together to work together in a way that was rational, created a synergy between the new inventions that were coming on and public safety, preserving innovation in America and public safety.
We have to do that again.

Well, we haven't been working on that because the President says his agreement is “morally binding” with these guys that are themselves saying that their own technology creates an existential risk to humanity.
We could have spent the time fixing our broken healthcare system, which is just becoming more and more and more expensive, in part, because of the President's policies.
We could be dealing with our broken immigration system, reintroduce ourselves to the idea that we live in a nation of laws and we live in a nation of immigrants.
We do, and we have been both at the greatest moments in this country's history.
I am sorry to say we haven't done any of that.
I mentioned education earlier.
I mentioned our literacy rates in this Nation that are the lowest they have been for 30 years.
So now we are going into this recess.
We have all come out here this afternoon to do our procedural motions on this floor about various things that we didn't get done.

But what we didn't get done is anything to make the American people's lives a little bit better, to deal with the burdens of cost and expense that our farmers and ranchers in Colorado are facing and every small business owner in Colorado is facing, that the next generation all over America is so worried about that they don't even know whether they are going to have a future of opportunity in this country, in the land of opportunity.
They don't know whether we have abandoned permanently the obligation that each generation of Americans has to create more opportunity, not less, for the people coming after it.
They don't know.
In fact, they doubt it.

They doubt it because what they see is the economic catastrophe of the way the economy is working--not just under President Trump but for decades and now much worse under President Trump--and the political chaos that we are leaving behind.
That is part of our legacy as well, unless we are going to figure out a way to come together on these fundamental issues and make some hard decisions here and focus attention on the next generation.
I have said many times that I don't blame Donald Trump for being elected President.
I am sorry that he was, but I don't blame him for being elected.
He won.
But the rest of us that don't want to go down this road anymore on the American people's behalf have to find a different path.

We have got to find a way to give each other hope in this country that we can make progress; that we can build an economy that, when it grows, it grows for everybody, not just the people at the very top; that we can have a Tax Code that actually supports work instead of passive investment, instead of just the assets that go up every time we pass a bill around here that wastes more trillions of dollars of the American people's tax money.
I am optimistic about that.
I am not optimistic in this moment because we are leaving the Senate floor without having done it.

I am not optimistic at this moment because Donald Trump is more focused on putting gild stuff on the walls of the Oval Office; putting his name on the Kennedy Center; building a ballroom; building a new triumphal arch in Washington, DC; breaking the Reflecting Pool; his own crypto.
He is more focused on that than he is on the issues that we need to focus on.
But there is nobody here who is surprised about that.
He is not doing anything he didn't say he would do.

We need to find a way to create confidence in the American people so we can build a politics that is not just about chaos and division, that is not just about fanning the flames but is actually about embracing the next generation and our responsibility to them, our obligation to them--and I would say to this country--to fulfill and to live up to the example that our parents and grandparents set for us and to make sure we get this right before we move on.
That is what we need to do, and I believe we will.
I appreciate the indulgence of the Presiding Officer.
I am sorry to have gone on so long tonight.
I thank the Presiding Officer for the time, and I thank my colleagues for giving me the chance to speak on the floor.
I yield the floor.

docs.title: Protect College Sports Act of 2026
s: Madam President, over the past few weeks, familiar scenes have been playing out in Colorado and all across the country.
Families are buying new books and backpacks, picking up school supplies, and taking their children to the pediatrician for their annual checkup.
For decades, back-to-school season did not prompt anxiety or confusion--except for maybe the kids like me that didn't do their summer reading.
Parents could rely on the recommendations from their pediatricians, and the questions they did have were answered by professionals.

But that peace of mind is being undermined by the current administration--including by the President of the United States and the Secretary of Health and Human Services, who have worked tirelessly to undermine decades of settled science around routine vaccinations that have kept kids safe in this country and around the world for years.
The consequences of that broken trust are showing up in our emergency rooms and in our classrooms.
Parents are increasingly concerned that their kids will go to school and come back with a serious disease.
Right now, our Nation is living through the most severe measles outbreak in over 35 years.
Measles is not a mild childhood inconvenience; it is one of the most contagious viruses on Earth, capable of causing high fevers, brain swelling, long-term disability, and death.
In Colorado, we have already confirmed 25 cases this year, including 7 hospitalizations.
Of these cases, 22 people were unvaccinated.
Of the 25 who have measles in Colorado today, 22 were unvaccinated.
That is the most we have had in over 30 years.
You have to go back to 1995 to find an outbreak in my State that is even close to what we are seeing today.
We are going backward when it comes to public health in the richest country in the world, and families in Colorado and all across this country are suffering the consequences.
But what is taking place in Colorado is especially tragic because Colorado's experience is one of the reasons that the United States has a two-dose vaccine recommendation today.
Back in 1988, an outbreak of 84 measles cases swept through Fort Lewis College in Durango.
It caught public health officials completely by surprise because nearly every student on that campus had already received a measles shot.

Under the guidance at that time, one dose was supposed to be enough, so CDC researchers--not people playing politics--CDC researchers went to Durango to figure out what exactly had gone wrong, to learn from this surprising outcome.

There, they discovered something that continues to inform our vaccine policy even today: While the virus infected students who had only received a single shot, not a single student who had had two doses got sick.
That campus in Durango became the proving ground for today's recommendation on measles.

Based directly on what they saw at Fort Lewis and similar outbreaks at that time, the CDC updated its guidelines in 1989 to establish the two-dose MMR schedule recommended for every schoolchild in America today.
This updated recommendation paved the way for measles to be officially eliminated across the United States in the year 2000.

That was a quarter of a century ago, when, following the science, this country eliminated measles; and for 30 years after that, routine vaccine recommendations have kept children safe and in the classroom.

Back then, faced with a public health emergency, we did what you would expect: We followed the evidence, updated our practices, and successfully prevented another outbreak of that scale or severity going forward.
We learned from each other.
Today, we are taking the opposite approach.

Instead of defending the settled science that saved millions of lives, President Trump and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., have spent months waging a campaign to promote skepticism, stoke fear, and amplify outright lies.
Look at what has happened in just the last few weeks.
In August, President Trump signed an Executive order on childhood vaccines that overrides decades of settled scientific consensus.
It encourages States to abandon school entry requirements.
It recommends reducing the number of routine vaccines protecting our kids.
And it calls for breaking up longstanding combination shots like the measles, mumps, and rubella--MMR--vaccine into separate single-disease doses spread over multiple doctor visits.
That recommendation ignores the basic, undeniable fact, which is that separate single-disease shots for measles, mumps, and rubella do not even exist in the U.S. market today.
They are so obsolete, and we were following the science, such that those single shots that the President and the HHS Secretary are calling for don't even exist today.
And it ignores the evidence that we have from countries that have already tried to separate the dose and then reverted back because it didn't work.
In the 1990s, Japan moved away from the combination MMR shot and attempted to separate the vaccines.
The result was predictable.
It was immediate and disastrous.
They saw vaccination rates plummet and measles outbreaks surged.
And, earlier this year, Japan officially abandoned the experiment--as we will, undoubtedly--and returned to the combined MMR vaccine.
We don't need to repeat another nation's mistake when the safety and lives of American children are on the line.
And telling parents to ask for shots that don't exist today only plunges families into further chaos.
It forces parents to schedule endless appointments, take time off work, and pay multiple copays for vaccines that used to be delivered safely in a single visit.
As everybody in this place knows, before I came to the Senate, I was the superintendent of schools in Denver.
This was such a happy time every year, when people were coming back, bringing their kids back to school.
And the last thing that they wanted to worry about was getting a free vaccine for their children or whether they should have that vaccine at all.

In those days, not that long ago, there was nobody worrying about a President or an HHS Secretary peddling misinformation that would lead to the biggest outbreak in measles that we have had in 30 years.
Things are hard enough as it is for families in Colorado and all across this country right now.
We don't need to make matters worse by intentionally misleading them about what is safe and making it harder for them to get a free vaccine at the pharmacy down the street.
And, by the way, I know my colleagues here well enough to understand something that I don't think the administration understands.
It is not good enough just to get your kid vaccinated.
The other kids in the school need to be vaccinated.
The other kids in the classroom need to be vaccinated for vaccines to work.
And, until this administration, that wasn't controversial because we could see what the science told us.

And for families in rural Colorado, where healthcare access is already stretched thin and local hospitals are already in danger of going bankrupt because of the razor-thin margins, this burden that they are creating is almost unbearable.

And to make matters worse, the other week, the President told the American people that the MMR vaccine--a safe, lifesaving shot given to hundreds of millions of children over four decades--the President called it “quite lethal”--“quite lethal.”
They had to send out Dr. Oz to clean up the record after that--the Director of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid.
They had to send him out on live television to contradict the President of the United States, who said that this routine vaccine that we have relied upon to save millions of lives was “quite lethal.”
Meanwhile, Secretary Kennedy spent last week serving as the keynote speaker for an anti-vax convention.

In the middle of the worst measles surge our country has seen in 35 years, the Nation's top health official stood in front of a crowd of anti-science activists and reassured them that they have “a strong and steadfast friend in the White House.”

I wish I could tell families trying to get their kids back to school that they have a steadfast friend in the White House, that they have somebody who is trying to make their life easier, not harder; to make it easier to bring up a kid, not harder.

When the leadership of HHS spends its time amplifying conspiracy theories, they are not making communities safer; they are driving down immunization rates, leaving our schools vulnerable, and putting the lives of Colorado's children directly in harm's way.
Today, Colorado has the sixth lowest measles vaccination rate in the nation for kindergartners.
Only 87.7 percent of Colorado kindergartners have received both doses of their MMR vaccine, and that is well below the 95 percent threshold for herd immunity.
In fact, 57 out of Colorado's 64 counties now fail to meet that basic safety line.
My message to Colorado parents from this floor tonight is simple: Vaccines are safe, they are effective, and they remain our strongest defense against diseases like measles.
And when we allow misinformation to drive down vaccination rates, we aren't just failing to meet an important public health indicator; we are failing moms in Aurora and in Pueblo and in Durango.

We are failing pediatricians like Dr. Stinar in Grand Junction, who are fighting on the frontlines of this disease; and we are failing vulnerable children across Colorado who have no choice in the matter.
Parents, pediatricians, and families across Colorado should be able to expect more from their government.
They deserve certainty.
They deserve clear communication.
They deserve to know that their public health system is designed to keep them safe, rather than to pursue another political agenda that has nothing to do with their education or their health.

I think we should be having a debate in this country about the state of healthcare in the United States of America and about the ways in which we failed this generation and the next generation in providing a system that actually delivers better healthcare at a reasonable price and mental health care at a reasonable price, instead of plunging people into further misery or into bankruptcy.
I wish we were having that debate on the Senate floor, but we can't begin to have that until the basic facts about science and medicine are taken seriously by this administration.
The President should start by rescinding his Executive order today on childhood vaccines.
He should fire Secretary Kennedy, as I have long called for.
But until that happens--and I don't think it is going to happen in the foreseeable future.
Until that happens, we are going to be stuck fighting battles against a disease that we functionally eliminated 30 years ago.
Kids and families in Colorado and all across this country deserve so much better than that.
I yield the floor.
I suggest the absence of a quorum.

docs.title: S. Res. 139
s: Mr. President, today, I am bringing the Congressional Review Act resolution to the floor to challenge EPA's disapproval of Colorado's regional haze plan.
I want to thank my colleagues Senator Hickenlooper and Senator Whitehouse for joining me in this effort.
For decades, we have relied on a simple principle in this country to keep our air clean: States and the Federal Government work together to reduce pollution and protect public health.
That includes programs like Regional Haze, which is designed to improve visibility in national parks and wilderness areas, like Rocky Mountain National Park in Northern Colorado.
In 2022, Colorado submitted a good-faith plan to improve air quality.
The State provided a range of solutions--including the voluntary, already-planned retirement of aging coal plants.
The decisions to close these plants were driven by basic economics.
Colorado utilities recognized that it no longer made sense to keep them open, based on the high costs of maintaining and operating.
And so in its regional haze plan, Colorado incorporated these previously made decisions into the State's strategy to reduce air pollution.
But EPA rejected Colorado's plan--not because it failed to meet Federal standards.
EPA rejected it because President Trump is laser- focused on keeping even aging coal plants operational, regardless of the costs or the desires of the local communities.
EPA's disapproval of Colorado's plan was based on an unprecedented and flawed legal theory.

EPA alleges that under section 110 of the Clean Air Act, Colorado must somehow prove these coal plant requirements would not violate the Constitution's takings clause, or, in other words, not constitute an illegal government seizure of private property.
But that is an impossible case for the State to make.
It is also not, in fact, what section 110 of the Clean Air Act requires or what Congress ever intended.
And to make matters worse, the EPA made this shift without any meaningful public input.
And the consequences of President Trump and Lee Zeldin's actions are real.
They are real for Colorado and for the West and for this country.
They are making it harder--harder--for Colorado to chart our own path on the energy transition and trying to force Coloradans to pay tens of millions of dollars to keep outdated coal plants running.
And they are doing this at a moment when energy prices have already increased as a result of the administration's own reckless actions.
Since President Trump's unprovoked war, gasoline prices have risen over 30 percent in Colorado.
They have cut investments in the cheapest types of electricity, while promoting the most expensive.

Everything the administration has done has made it harder for parents in Colorado to pay their bills and heat their homes, and now to take their children to enjoy some of the incredible national parks and public lands our State has to offer.
If this ruling stands, it won't stop in Colorado.

It could open the door to similar challenges across the country, weakening air quality protections and leaving States in an impossible position--responsible for results but stripping them of the tools and the authority to achieve them.
And so I urge my colleagues to support S.J. Res.
139 to overturn the EPA's decision.
I ask consent to yield back all time.
I ask for the yeas and nays.

docs.title: Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act: Resumed
s: Thank you, Madam President.
May I be recognized after Senator Merkley, Madam President?
Thank you, Madam President.
Madam President, I thank the Presiding Officer for the recognition.
I spent last weekend in Grand Junction.
I am happy to be here tonight on the floor with my colleague from Colorado John Hickenlooper.
I spent last weekend in Grand Junction, in our State, on Colorado's Western Slope.
And my conversations with young parents and with families just starting out, I think--I would hope--would be familiar to many colleagues that are here.

We discussed the price of housing, which has surged over 80 percent over the last 10 years in Colorado; the price of healthcare, which is ratcheting higher and becoming impossible for families to afford, not just in Colorado but all across our country; the cost of childcare, which is making it harder for families to live any semblance of a middle-class life--families that are working two jobs just to pay the mortgage can't even afford childcare when they are working with those two salaries--and our inability as a nation, as a State, to prepare our kids for the dynamic and potentially hugely unforgiving economy they are about to enter.
This is a tough economy that we are in today, and tariffs and now gas prices haven't helped.
Last week, colleagues, I met with a food bank from El Paso County, who told me that they stay open late--listen to this, U.S. Senate.

This food bank in El Paso County said that they stay open late 1 day a week to have teachers' night so the teachers that have worked all week teaching children have the opportunity to come to that food bank in the evening to get food to feed their own children at home.
I doubt very much that there is a living American who can remember a decade in this country when we took it for granted that teachers would have to go to a food bank to feed their own children.

Can you imagine, in the 1950s, in this Chamber, if it were known that people teaching in America--in inner-city America or in the suburbs of our great cities--that the pay wasn't satisfactory, so they had to go to a food bank after work?

And that is happening to working people all over our country, people that are in what we think of as traditional middle-class lives, because of how savage this economy has been, because of the affordability crisis that, I will say, has been with us for decades in this country but the current administration, the Trump administration, has made far worse and now is making it even worse with what they are doing to energy prices because of their unauthorized war in the Middle East.
I wish we were working on that affordability crisis today.
I wish we were working on building an economy that worked for everybody, not just the people at the very top.

This is a choice that is being made by President Trump and the majority in this Senate, the Republicans, who have spent the entire week fighting for a bill that will make it harder for family members and for aging parents and for their cousins to vote or to register to vote.
That is what they have chosen to use the floor of the U.S. Senate to do.
It is shameful.

It is shameful both because it is ignoring the affordability crisis that our families are facing, but it is shameful because there is no excuse for taking away the right to vote from people all over the United States of America.
These are people who are supposed to believe in States' rights, believe in the ability of States to be able to run their own affairs.
And Donald Trump--President Trump--and the Republican's SAVE America Act rewrites the way we run elections in America completely.
It rips up the processes all over the United States of America at the local level that county clerks and election officials understand.
It requires the Federal Government to have access to the voter rolls, a shocking thing from the party that is supposed to be about States' rights.
And it creates yet another unfunded mandate for States and for local communities.
There is no money in here to fund the stuff that is in this bill.
Most troublingly, it imposes new document requirements for voter registration that many Americans do not have or do not have access to.
Madam President, 146 million Americans don't have a passport.
Almost 70 million women do not have a birth certificate that matches their real name.
That should be self-evident to anybody in this Chamber, but it is ignored completely by the people who wrote this legislation.
Over 8 million Americans have moved to a different State within the last year, and an average of over 17 million will have moved counties.
Many of them--probably most--do not have the paperwork that this bill requires.
That doesn't make any sense.
These people aren't trying to evade the law.
These people are availing themselves of their right as an American citizen to move from place to place in this Nation.
This radical legislation actually requires people to register in- person, banning common methods, as we heard from the Senator from Alaska who is standing up for her State as she always does.
We should be supporting her.
We should be supporting Alaska's way of running their elections rather than imposing Donald Trump's corrupt way of running his elections.
This radical legislation actually requires people to register in- person, banning common methods of registration--online registration, through the mail, or automatically at the DMV.
That is how 94 percent of Americans register to vote.
Many of them are seniors.
Many of them live in rural communities.

I would like to see the majority party in this Chamber come to western Colorado and try to take--rather than having this fake filibuster--try to actually take mail-in ballots from the people of western Colorado.
I would like to see that.
They would avail themselves of any means necessary to prevent that from happening.
The SAVE America Act would set our voter registration process back decades.
If you are one of the more than 60 million Americans who live in rural areas, you might now need to drive hundreds of miles to stand in line at a local election agency.
If you live overseas, you will have to fly back.
If you don't have a passport, you better have your birth certificate.

If you don't have your birth certificate or you changed your name like tens of millions of married women across this country living in the 21st century, you will have to provide additional documents and sign affidavits.
All of this will--
I will not yield.
I will not yield.
I have waited an hour--
Mr. LEE.--inaccuracy on the bill.
You will have your time.
Thank you, Madam President.
Thank you, Madam President.
Madam President, I will yield for the one inaccuracy you think that I have--
Well, then you will have to wait.
Then you will have to wait.
Then you will have to wait.
Madam President, I haven't yielded the floor.
I didn't.
I said I would yield for one inaccuracy.
That is all I said.
I am not willing to hear it.
I am not willing to hear it.
I will hear it after--
I don't believe I did yield.
If I did yield--
I will exercise my right to withdraw.
Madam President, all of this will have to be done in-person.
Kansas tried to implement its own State-level version of President Trump's SAVE America Act in 2013 with disastrous results.
This law, which included citizenship documentation requirements, ended up blocking the voter registration of more than 31,000 U.S. citizens who are otherwise eligible to vote.
That represented about 12 percent of all Kansas voter registrations during that period.
Even Kansas Republican secretary of state who championed the bill when he was a State legislator has warned against the bill now before us.
He has warned against the bill now before us saying: It didn't work out so well.
And Kansas law was blocked by a Federal court, as it should have been.
If we pass this bill, we will have now two different election--Madam President, can I have the floor without the interruption of my colleague from Utah?
If you guys are done, I would like to--Madam President, I would like--
Madam President, if we pass this bill, we will now have two different election regimes in this country--one for Federal elections and one for local elections.
That is insane in and of itself and begs the question: Why does Donald Trump want to pass this bill?
He wants to run roughshod over our election system because he claims there is an epidemic of voter fraud caused by undocumented people voting.
That is at the heart of his claim, and that has been the heart of his claim throughout two Presidential elections and this Presidency.
The problem is that he is blowing up our elections, and there is no evidence to support his claim of fraud.
The fact is that even his own Department of Homeland Security used by many States to verify voter citizenship returned .04 percent of voter participants as noncitizens.
A bipartisan policy center analysis of the Heritage Foundation's debate of noncitizen voting found only 77 cases in 25 years of nearly 2 billion votes cast.
And individual States tell us the same.
We heard it earlier tonight.
Last year, Utah performed a citizen review of its entire voter registration list.
There was no noncompliance.
After an assessment of more than 2 million registered voters, Utah identified only 1 confirmed instance of noncitizen registration and no instances of noncitizen voting.
We definitely have a crisis in our democracy and in our economy and they are related.
Over the decades, we have suffered through an economy that has reduced economic mobility and hollowed out America's middle class.

At the same time, we have built a tax system that disproportionately benefits those who own assets and perpetuates the inequalities that accumulated with generational wealth, a tax system that allows Donald Trump and Elon Musk to pass their stock portfolios onto their heirs without paying a dollar on the gains that they have accrued.
That is a crisis.
The lack of economic mobility is a crisis, and I am sorry to say that that tax regime, that has been done in a bipartisan manner.

Republicans definitely more than Democrats have pursued trickle-down economics, but Democrats and Republicans both played a role creating an unfair system that reinforces our desperate lack of economic mobility and concretizes our deep and growing economic inequality.

At the same time, this body has failed to make important investment in our infrastructure while saddling future generations with ever- greater amounts of debt, debt whose service costs will now predictably take up $1 trillion of our annual budget in interest--more than we spend on Medicare or defense, a higher share of the economy than at any point in American history.
We are in a dangerous moment at home and abroad.
There is no doubt about that.

And at the same time as Coloradans and Americans across the country are struggling to get by, as teachers are going to those food banks to feed their own children, when confidence in our institutions and in our politics is at record lows, and we have a campaign finance system that gives inordinate power to the wealthiest.
Tonight is not the night to go through how wrongly decided Citizens United was, how wrongly decided, how ignorant that decision was of the way politics actually works in this country.
But let me just point out to you that in 2008, before Citizens United was decided, the top 100 individual donors contributed a combined $80 million--$80 million in 2008.
That is what the 100 donors contributed.
In 2024, the top 10 donors--the top 10 donors--contributed over $1.2 billion.
Spending by outside groups has exploded from a total of $574 million in 2008 to almost $4.5 billion in that last election, an increase of 8 times--8 times.
No one could possibly believe that the amount of money--that that amount of money is helping our democracy.
Let me tell you something: Does the SAVE Act do anything about that corrosiveness in our politics?
Of course not.
Of course not.
And let me tell you something that was a fatal flaw in the Supreme Court's decision while I am here.
Maybe the pages, when they are Senators, will be able to fix this problem because we sure aren't going fix it.

At the end of that--at the end of their decision, they said: By the way, if the Congress ever passes a constitutional regulation of--in their words--constitutional regulation of the outside spending in our political system, we will, of course, have to give that the proper analysis, the proper--excuse me--the required constitutional analysis.

Of course, nobody will ever pass that around here because the billionaires that are writing checks to these elections just have to rattle the pennies in their pockets and the change in their pockets and threaten to run a primary against anybody in this place, and the bill won't be brought.
And then there is a profound corruption of inaction that sets in as a result to our legislative branch both here and in the House of Representatives.
Does the SAVE America Act address any of this?
Of course not.
Instead, Donald Trump and the Republicans have brought to the floor a bill to make it harder for ordinary American citizens to register and to vote.

Fundamentally, the SAVE America Act is an astonishing Federal overreach in search of a scandal that doesn't exist and would have the effect of undermining fraud-free elections like we have in Colorado.
Colorado was the first State in America to complete a risk-limiting audit, the gold standard for verifying the integrity of election results.
It entails counting and comparing a representative sample of ballots to the reported result.
To prevent hacking, none of our voting machines are connected to the internet.
We require county clerks to use two- factor authentication to access voter databases.
Once a vote is cast, a bipartisan team of election judges in each county checks every signature against the copy in the database for any discrepancies.
All election officials and judges with access to the tabulation process must first pass a Colorado Bureau of Investigation background check.
And Colorado has spent years--years--implementing top-tier cyber security measures and audits to prevent hackers from interfering in our electoral process.
We should be modeling our Federal system off the gold standard framework we have in Colorado, a national leader in terms of voter access, election security, and might I say, voter turnout.
Instead, the SAVE America Act would eliminate--eliminate, outlaw--many of the practices that Colorado has adopted to keep our elections safe and increase voter confidence.
How dare you?
It would end Colorado's mail-in and online voter registration system.
It would force Colorado to increase the security risks of our voter data and routinely purge voter rolls.
It would push experienced county clerks and election workers out of the field.
It would remove the possibility of using a number of State IDs when going to vote.

It would create two tiers of voting for Federal and State elections and possibly upend our mail-in ballot system itself by requiring that every Coloradan proactively request a ballot and resubmit proof of ID alongside their ballot request in every election.
Colorado already has ID requirements when casting a ballot.
We already have among the cleanest voter rolls in this country.
We don't need Donald Trump to corrupt our process.
Even the Heritage Foundation ranked us as second in the Nation in 2020 for clean lists--the Heritage Foundation.
We have one of the most secure election systems of any State in our country, and because Coloradans have trust in our elections, we have some of the highest voter turnouts in the country.
But the SAVE America Act--the so-called SAVE America Act--does not bring our system anywhere close to what we enjoy in Colorado.
Instead it turns into a dark but familiar pattern in American history.
And I am sorry to say, but this bill before us is just another in a long line of legislative efforts to limit the franchise in this country, to add new restrictions and additional obstacles.
Nobody wants voter fraud.
I do not want voter fraud.
I come from a State where there is no voter fraud.
We set the gold standard, in part because of the work my colleague John Hickenlooper did when he was Governor of Colorado.
This is a pretext.
This is a pretext to invade our elections.
I know my colleague from Texas wants to speak.
So I am trying to skip ahead here.

We have had a fight over many, many, many years in this Nation to broaden the franchise, from the very beginning, and that fight was won by men and women who marched to demand that their vote count equally in this country, no matter what color they were, no matter where they lived in our Nation, no matter what education or religion their parents had or whether their parents were immigrants to this country.

In this modern era, when one of the real fundamental risks to our democracy is the American people's loss of confidence in our institutions, including our voting process and elections themselves, we now have a group of people who are trying to create political advantage for themselves by restricting the vote in the name of addressing a mythical voter fraud that does not exist.
The American people will not be fooled by this.
They will be angry about this, as they should.
The American people have come to rely on vote-by-mail, and registration by mail, and early voting.
They believe our system is fraud free, and where it is not, the State should address it.
Our citizens have come to rely on having the franchise extended through modern technology and modern practices.

Nobody I know in Colorado has said they doubt the validity or veracity of our voting system--no matter what party they are in or whether they live in rural Colorado or urban Colorado--or the importance of the ability to register online, or for students and others to have the benefit of same-day registration.
I wish everybody in this country had the benefit of that.
Those are ways of encouraging participation in our democracy.
None of us want fraud.
None of us want fraud.
And there is no fraud.
The good news is there is certainly no evidence in Colorado or across the country that that fraud exists.

And this is the most sweeping effort, make no mistake, by Donald Trump, by the Republicans here in the Senate, to “nationalize our elections,” to undermine voter confidence, and inject new chaos into a system he is terrified will turn against him; to make life harder for Americans that he thinks voted against him, and probably will make it harder for the people who voted for him.
Since the President's return to office, he has focused relentlessly on false narratives of voter fraud.
He has issued Executive orders that are unenforceable.
He has sued States that have refused to comply and threatened to take control of the electoral process in States he views as political enemies.
He has sent Federal agents from the FBI and the Director of National Intelligence to seize ballots in Georgia, election records in Arizona, and voting machines in Puerto Rico.
His Justice Department has sued 30 States, including Colorado, demanding sensitive, unredacted voter data to create a national voter database.
And President Trump has pursued a longstanding and inexplicable grievance against mail-in voting, which he falsely claims can be used to commit mass amounts of fraud.
It is simply not true.
It is simply not true.
He sees it, in his own words--the SAVE America Act--as a method to “guarantee the midterms” this November.
He sees, in his own words, the SAVE America Act as a method to “guarantee the midterms” this November.
And that is why they put this on this floor now?
I hope not.
I really hope not.
This is an election bill that distorts our shared understanding of what free and fair elections should look like, and Coloradans want no part of it.
This legislation, by the way, is wildly unpopular in America.
We have received thousands of calls and letters in opposition to the SAVE America Act.
We received over 7,000 last month alone.
Madam President, I ask unanimous consent that these constituent letters be printed in the Record.
The Founders understood the gravity of the debate before them about who could and who could not claim the franchise.
The authors of Federalist No. 52 explain that “the definition of the right of suffrage is very justly regarded as a fundamental article of republican government.”
They wrestled with this question.
They wrestled with this question.
They debated it.
And, ultimately, they excluded the great number of subjects who were newly made Americans, but, nevertheless, were denied, as those at Seneca Falls wrote, “the first right of citizen.”
This was the founding generation's great mistake--this and the enslavement of Americans.
And we have spent centuries working to rectify it--centuries working to rectify it.
Should the SAVE America Act pass, we will fall further away from realizing this country's promise and retread the familiar errors of the past.
We should reject that vision of our democracy.
We should reject that return to a history that we have fought so hard to free ourselves from.
Coloradans and all Americans deserve better than this.
I yield the floor and look forward to hearing my colleague from Texas.

docs.title: Finish the Arkansas Valley Conduit Act
s: Last week, President Trump vetoed H.R. 131, the Finish the Arkansas Valley Conduit Act, a bill that passed both Chambers of Congress unanimously with broad bipartisan support.
The President did not veto this bill for any substantive objection.
He did so out of a desire to punish the State that he believes didn't support him politically.
In my opinion, this is the last reason any President should make a decision about anything.
An election is one thing, but once we hold office, we have a responsibility to represent every American, regardless of their political party, regardless of their politics.

The President's veto will inflict real harm on people in my State by denying 50,000 Coloradans living in tiny rural towns across the Arkansas River Valley and southeastern Colorado access to clean, affordable drinking water.
Those farmers and ranchers have been forced to rely on unsafe, carcinogenic water for generations, despite the Federal Government's six-decade-old commitment to fix their water infrastructure.
The Arkansas Valley Conduit is the final unfinished piece of a water delivery project that Congress authorized in 1962, 2 years before I was even born.
The conduit would wind its way for 130 miles, from Pueblo, CO, to the State line, traversing farming communities that had to rely on bottled water or prohibitively expensive water treatment.
This area covers a quarter of the land mass of Colorado.

It is sprinkled with small towns and populated with small business owners and farmers and ranchers who are dedicated to a rural way of life, who have been fighting--generation after generation after generation--to try to bring this clean water to their valley but are living in fear that they or their children are delivering poisonous water.

There are probably not a lot of Senators here who aren't confident that the water that is consumed by their children or their grandchildren--the water that is consumed in their neighborhoods or part of their State--isn't safe.
That, I think, would be a reasonable expectation in the richest country in the world.

Yet the inability of us to be able to finish this project--this joint project--has made it impossible for the hard-working people in southeastern Colorado to have the benefit--a benefit that other people just take for granted because they live maybe closer to a city or in a wealthier area than where the people in the Arkansas Valley live.

For 64 years, Coloradans have been relying on Washington to fulfill its promise to build on their efforts--they have been a big part of this in southeastern Colorado--to build on their efforts to deliver clean drinking water.
The effort to complete the conduit has always been a partnership between the Federal and local government, driven by the leadership of the Southeastern Colorado Water Conservancy District.

In the face of rising costs and materials and labor, once again, southeastern Coloradans, just as the generations before them have, came together to put forward an inventive solution to lower costs by changing the project's financing, with no increase at all to the Federal obligation here.

The House passed the Arkansas Valley Conduit Act last July, and the Senate passed it just 3 weeks ago, with the support of every single Member of Congress--every Member of the House, every Member of the Senate.
There is almost nothing that ever gets through with that kind of universal bipartisan support.

Republicans and Democrats, under the leadership of Representatives Lauren Boebert and Jeff Hurd, my colleagues from Colorado, and Senator Hickenlooper, my colleague here in the U.S. Senate, we all worked together to ensure that rural Colorado would finally have access to clean drinking water, something every American should reasonably expect.
And the folks in southeastern Colorado deserve it just as much as anybody else does.
Instead, when it got to his desk, President Trump used his first Presidential veto of his second term to deny Coloradans what should be a fundamental right as an American.
Article I of the Constitution explicitly provides Congress with the power to override a Presidential veto.
Although overrides should only be used when necessary, they are essential when both Chambers of Congress have spoken clearly and spoken unanimously.

There are very few places in the Constitution where the Founders actually themselves wrote about having a supermajority vote in the Chambers of Congress, and this is one of those things, because while they believed that a veto override should be rare, they believed that it was an essential part of this branch of the Federal Government exercising its oversight when a President does something like veto the Arkansas Valley Conduit, which is wildly out of step with what the people that we represent want all across this country.
If Congress allows this veto to stand, we set a troubling precedent.
It would mean that noncontroversial, bipartisan bills that pass without objection can be rejected for reasons wholly unrelated to the substance and be weaponized politically.
It is no secret--and I am sorry to come to this floor to have to say this--that President Trump is, at the moment, engaged in a political vendetta against the State of Colorado.
I don't think any President should be engaged in a vendetta against any State--obviously, least of all, the State that I represent.

But what I worry about more than anything is that this is going to become a normal practice around here, which it hasn't been until now, where Presidents reward the States that support them and punish the States that haven't politically.
That is not how we should run this democracy.
That is not how the Founders of this country wrote the Constitution.
They didn't even think there would be political parties.

They felt that it was very important for Congress to be able to be the backstop at a moment when, for whatever reason, a President made a decision that didn't serve the American people properly or well.

If we can't overcome this veto, I think it would say that no bill is safe and that the efforts of every single elected Member of Congress would now be at risk to one person's view and one person's decision.
Later today, I am pleased to say the House is considering whether to override the President's veto.
They are putting it on the floor of the House.
I congratulate the work of Congresswoman Boebert and Congressman Hurd and the rest of the Colorado House delegation to work with the Speaker to get this on the floor of the House.
It is absolutely critical for the people of Colorado that Congress act, that we support, once again, the Arkansas Valley Conduit, which we have unanimously.
Next week, this bill will come over to the Senate floor.

I urge every single Member of the Senate to do what you did the last time, which is to support with your vote the 50,000 farmers and ranchers in southeastern Colorado who need the benefit of this clean water.
They are not asking, by the way, for a handout here.
They have done their part, generation, after generation, after generation, to keep this project alive.
They have done their part to get a unanimous vote in the House of Representatives and on the floor of this Senate to be able to keep their faith with their children and their grandchildren.
The least we can do in this Senate is to uphold the work that they have done and also the Constitution of the United States of America.

I hope every person in this room will use this as an opportunity to stand with the people in southeastern Colorado; to stand with our Constitution; and to make sure that we all--all--take seriously the legislative responsibility we have as an independent branch of government.
I yield the floor.
